grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Quero entrar, mas não posso abrir o portão. Por que? Porque a chave está com a vizinha.

Porque a chave está com a vizinha.
Por que vocês querem o pátio?

grammar.note_en:
Poder and querer are different verbs. Poder expresses being able to do something, and in a request or rule can express permission. Querer expresses wanting or willingness. The neighbor says Quero emprestar o pátio, mas não posso abrir o portão (“I want to lend the courtyard, but I cannot open the gate”). He is willing to share it; the main-gate key is elsewhere. Later the female owner says Não quero emprestar a chave (“I do not want to lend the key”). Her refusal is a choice about her property, not a claim that she physically lacks her key. Do not translate both negatives as the same obstacle.

The actual present forms are posso, pode, podemos, podem (“I can; you/he/she can; we can; plural you/they can”) and quero, quer, queremos, querem (“I want; you/he/she wants; we want; plural you/they want”). Both verbs are irregular in their encountered patterns; do not build posso from a guessed regular ending. Posso ir ao mercado means “I can go to the market”; queremos pedir o pátio means “we want to ask for the courtyard”; elas querem começar means “they want to begin.” A named singular subject and você use pode/quer; plural eles/elas/vocês use podem/querem. The subject can remain implicit when the dialogue identifies it.

After these modals, the next verb uses its infinitive, the dictionary/action-label form ending in -ar, -er or -ir. It does not agree a second time with the subject: posso abrir (“I can open”), podemos abrir (“we can open”), pode entrar (“you/he/she can enter”), podem entrar (“they/you can enter”). The modal carries the person and number. The encountered infinitives now have real sentence use: pedir (“ask for”), emprestar (“lend”), seguir (“follow”), preparar (“prepare”), tirar (“remove”), colocar (“put”), levar (“carry”), começar (“begin”), abrir (“open”), entrar (“enter”), sair (“leave/exit”), ir (“go”), ler (“read”), ter (“have”) and estar (“be, for location/state”). This does not grant new verbs or unencountered tense patterns.

Permission is clear from its source. Vocês podem entrar com o vizinho means “You may enter with the neighbor”: the owner agrees to that access. Não podem deixar a entrada aberta means “You may not leave the entrance open,” a condition of use; the women are not physically incapable of leaving a door open. Não quero os livros no pátio agora means “I do not want the books in the courtyard now.” The final agora matters: the woman accepts the reading-night plan but wants preparation before the books arrive. Não queremos cadeiras na saída means “We do not want chairs in the exit,” not “we do not want any chairs at all.” Keep the scope of each negative attached to its actual action, object and context.

Por que at the start of these questions means “why”; porque gives the reason, “because.” Por que você não pode abrir? means “Why can’t you open [it]?”; Porque a chave está com a vizinha means “Because the key is with the female neighbor.” Por que vocês querem o pátio? means “Why do you want the courtyard?”; Porque as cadeiras não cabem juntas no café means “Because the chairs do not fit together in the café.” Por que você não quer emprestar a chave? means “Why don’t you want to lend the key?”; Porque eu preciso da chave means “Because I need the key.” The question form has two words, the reason conjunction one. These examples do not introduce unrestricted que complement or relative clauses.

Emprestar allows temporary use without transferring ownership: the co-owners keep the courtyard and their keys. The reference book is lent for reading and returned to its owner; it is not a gift. Pedir means asking for something: Ana pede a chave means “Ana asks for the key”; Bia pede o pátio means “Bia asks for the courtyard.” Aceitar and recusar mean accepting and refusing a proposal in this context. Bia pede o pátio; a vizinha aceita means “Bia asks for the courtyard; the woman accepts [the request].” Ana pede a chave; a vizinha recusa means “Ana asks for the key; the woman refuses [the request].” The woman does not receive the courtyard or refuse to receive a key: the preceding request supplies the omitted object. Aceitamos means “we accept.”

Portão is the large gate, while entrada and saída name the entrance and exit functions. The small doorway serves both functions here. Vizinha is a female neighbor, parallel to the male vizinho already known. Fácil/difícil means “easy/difficult.” O caminho é fácil means “The route is easy”; o mapa não é difícil means “The map is not difficult”; é difícil preparar uma noite com papéis na entrada means “It is difficult to prepare an evening with papers in the entrance.” Difficulty is not an absolute synonym of impossibility. Preparing the courtyard is accepted but remains work: one paper is removed as a demonstration, not the whole cleaning job. The written action sequence tirar papéis; colocar cadeiras; ler means “remove papers; put chairs in place; read.” These are infinitive action labels using forms already encountered with the modals; the sequence establishes the preparation order without introducing a new finite command or claiming the event has happened.

The newly encountered group forms são (“are”), precisam (“need”) and saem (“leave/exit”) correspond to the earlier singular é, precisa and sai. São is one of the specifically licensed irregular forms; the chapter does not infer a full paradigm from it.
